account: Pirotta and colleagues tested AI detection of marine wildlife in three-dimensional X-ray scans. Their paper of 8 June 2026 states that the scans were collected from September 2024 to February 2025. It reports 298 scans from 68 specimens, including preserved specimens and fresh shark material. The researchers expanded the scans by inserting specimen images into baggage images. A 512-bag test set contained both original scans and these synthetic composites, drawn from the same specimen population. Table 3 reports detection rates of 95% for shark fins, 96% for seahorses, and 86% for sea cucumbers. The overall false-alarm rate was 13%; the class-specific rates were 2%, 9%, and 1%. Rapiscan supplied equipment and funded staff participation in analysis and writing. The authors report laboratory detection only, and the paper reports no operational seizure or customs evaluation. Mongabay reported on 16 June 2026 that outside researchers and a spokesperson for the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) welcomed the study as a complementary tool. Toby Breckon of Durham University told Mongabay that major airports already have 3D scanners for hold luggage. Michelle Anagnostou of Oxford noted that the study left out sea freight. Pirotta told Mongabay that the next step is to share the method so that other species can be detected in other regions.

fields.account: Pirotta and colleagues tested AI detection of marine wildlife in three-dimensional X-ray scans. Their paper of 8 June 2026 states that the scans were collected from September 2024 to February 2025. It reports 298 scans from 68 specimens, including preserved specimens and fresh shark material. The researchers expanded the scans by inserting specimen images into baggage images. A 512-bag test set contained both original scans and these synthetic composites, drawn from the same specimen population. Table 3 reports detection rates of 95% for shark fins, 96% for seahorses, and 86% for sea cucumbers. The overall false-alarm rate was 13%; the class-specific rates were 2%, 9%, and 1%. Rapiscan supplied equipment and funded staff participation in analysis and writing. The authors report laboratory detection only, and the paper reports no operational seizure or customs evaluation. Mongabay reported on 16 June 2026 that outside researchers and a spokesperson for the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) welcomed the study as a complementary tool. Toby Breckon of Durham University told Mongabay that major airports already have 3D scanners for hold luggage. Michelle Anagnostou of Oxford noted that the study left out sea freight. Pirotta told Mongabay that the next step is to share the method so that other species can be detected in other regions.
fields.summary: In laboratory tests on real and synthetic CT scans, Rapiscan's AI algorithms detected shark fins, seahorses and sea cucumbers at 86–96%, with 13% overall false alarms; no customs use is reported.
